notes.meaning: Solomon began to love many women from neighboring pagan nations, in addition to his marriage to Pharaoh's daughter. Kings in the ancient world often married foreign princesses to secure political treaties and display their wealth. However, these choices openly violated God's rules for Israel's leaders and laid the groundwork for spiritual compromise.

God had clearly warned the Israelites never to intermarry with these nations because foreign spouses would lead them toward false gods. Despite having great wisdom, Solomon ignored this warning and bound himself to these women in romantic affection. Human wisdom alone cannot protect someone who chooses to ignore God's commands.

Solomon gathered seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines, who were secondary wives of lower legal standing. This enormous harem reflected the excessive luxury and political prestige common among eastern rulers. Just as Scripture warned, this vast number of foreign wives slowly pulled his affections away from the Lord.

As Solomon grew older, his wives persuaded him to honor other gods. His father David had committed serious sins, but David always repented and stayed entirely faithful to the Lord alone. In contrast, Solomon allowed his loyalty to become divided, showing that advancing years do not automatically make a person spiritually secure.

Solomon began to take part in the worship of Ashtoreth, the Sidonian goddess of fertility and war, and Milcom, the detestable god of the Ammonites. The Bible calls these idols abominations because their rituals were morally corrupt and even included child sacrifice. Honoring these dark religions was a tragic fall for a king blessed with divine wisdom.

Solomon committed evil in the sight of the Lord by failing to follow Him with a whole heart. Even if he continued to present offerings at the temple in Jerusalem, worshipping other deities ruined his obedience. God expects exclusive devotion, not a mixture of true faith with pagan superstition.

Solomon went so far as to build high places, which were open-air pagan altars, on the Mount of Olives just east of Jerusalem. There he accommodated Chemosh, the war god of Moab, and Molech, the Ammonite idol worshipped through burning children. Setting up these altars right opposite the temple was a direct insult to the presence of God.

Solomon built similar worship centers for all his foreign wives so that each could burn incense and offer sacrifices to her homeland's gods. In trying to satisfy every wife's desires, he turned the holy city into a center of pagan worship. Compromising on God's truth to please others steadily leads to deeper moral decay.

The Lord was intensely angry with Solomon because his heart had deserted the God of Israel. God had appeared to Solomon in person twice—first at Gibeon and later after the temple was finished—giving him unique privileges and personal assurances. Disobeying after receiving such clear spiritual experiences left the king without any excuse.

The Lord had explicitly instructed Solomon during those personal visits never to follow other gods. Solomon knew God's standard clearly, but he willfully brushed the warning aside. Sinning against direct light and knowledge always brings severe consequences.

God announced His sentence to Solomon, likely sending the message through a prophet. Because Solomon broke God's covenant—His solemn agreement and laws—the Lord promised to rip the kingdom away and give it to one of Solomon's subordinates. Worldly power quickly crumbles when God's favor is lost.

differ.view: Many in this tradition teach that Solomon was brought to repentance before his death, pointing to the book of Ecclesiastes as his confession of sorrow for sin.
Some believe Solomon died in apostasy (falling away from the faith), noting that 1 Kings records no repentance or spiritual recovery before his death.

notes.meaning: Out of love for David and the promises made to him, God decided not to divide the kingdom during Solomon's lifetime. The painful split would instead take place under the rule of Solomon's son. God's faithfulness to His covenant with David softened the immediate timing of the judgment, even though the consequence was certain.

The Lord promised not to take the entire kingdom away, but to leave one tribe for Solomon's son. This preserved the tribe of Judah, which absorbed Benjamin, so that David's royal line would continue in Jerusalem. Through this faithful remnant, God kept the royal lineage alive that would eventually bring the promised Messiah.

God began His discipline by raising up an adversary named Hadad, an Edomite prince. The word for adversary here is related to the word for opponent or rival. While Solomon stayed obedient, Israel enjoyed total peace, but his rebellion invited conflict back into the land.

Years earlier, King David and his army general Joab had conquered Edom, fighting for six months until they struck down its male soldiers. Joab stayed in the territory to bury the casualties and secure control. This ruthless war left the surviving Edomites nursing a deep desire for vengeance against Israel.

During the slaughter, royal servants rescued young Hadad and helped him flee toward Egypt. Even though he was only a small boy, God preserved his life amid the destruction. Decades later, this surviving prince would become the very person God used to trouble Solomon.

Hadad's servants led him through Midian and the wilderness of Paran, picking up traveling companions before reaching Egypt. The Egyptian Pharaoh welcomed the young prince, giving him a house, land, and regular food supplies. Pharaoh sheltered royal refugees like Hadad to keep political influence against neighboring nations.

Hadad gained great favor in Pharaoh's eyes as he grew into adulthood. To bring him fully into the royal circle, Pharaoh gave him the sister of Queen Tahpenes as his wife. God guided these circumstances so that Hadad would possess the prestige and resources needed to challenge Solomon later.

Hadad and his wife had a son named Genubath, a name that recalls someone taken away by stealth. Queen Tahpenes loved the child so much that she raised and weaned him right inside the palace alongside Pharaoh's own children. Hadad's family was now firmly established in the highest circles of Egyptian power.

News reached Egypt that King David had died and that his feared general Joab was also gone. With those powerful conquerors dead, Hadad asked Pharaoh for permission to return to Edom. He had never forgotten his homeland and wanted to reclaim his royal heritage.

Pharaoh asked what Hadad could possibly lack, since he enjoyed royal comfort and honor in Egypt. Hadad replied that he needed nothing, but still pleaded earnestly to be allowed to go home. All the luxuries of an empire could not quench his desire to return and fight for his people's independence.
